title: Toposort a tiny DAG
starter:
from dataclasses import dataclass

# A tiny DAG, given as a list of nodes. Every name appears once.
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Node:
    name: str
    srcs: tuple[str, ...]

# Return the names reachable from root, each exactly once, in depth-first
# post-order: visit a node's srcs left to right first, then the node itself.
# Every node comes after all of its sources.
def topo(graph: list[Node], root: str) -> list[str]:
    return [root]
hints: This is the same 'visit sources first, then the node' walk as the toposort stepper in lesson 0.3. Start with a recursive `go(name)`: if it's unseen, mark it, call `go` on each source left to right, then append the name.

Look nodes up in a dict built once, `{n.name: n for n in graph}`, not by scanning the list each time. Keep a `seen` set so a shared node is visited once. That's what makes the 31-level doubling DAG instant.

The last test is a chain 5000 nodes deep, past Python's default recursion limit of 1000. Either raise it with `sys.setrecursionlimit(10_000)`, or drop recursion: keep an explicit stack of `(name, finished)` pairs, and push `(name, True)` before the sources (in reverse) so the name is appended after them.

answer.explain: The reference walks with an explicit stack instead of recursion. Popping `(name, False)` marks the name seen, pushes `(name, True)`, then pushes the sources in reverse so the first source is handled first. Popping `(name, True)` appends the name. The seen set makes shared subgraphs cost one visit, and the explicit stack means a 5000-deep chain can't hit the recursion limit.
